back.body: BLOOD VOLUME RISES SUBSTANTIALLY → she can lose a LOT before her vitals move · BASELINE: heart rate a little HIGHER, pressure a little LOWER — different reference values · BLOOD IS DIVERTED AWAY FROM THE UTERUS BEFORE SHE SHOWS ANY SIGN — THE BABY SUFFERS FIRST, so NORMAL MATERNAL VITALS ARE NOT REASSURANCE ABOUT THE PREGNANCY · FROM MID-PREGNANCY, LYING FLAT COMPRESSES THE VEIN RETURNING BLOOD TO THE HEART → pressure falls from POSITION ALONE · TILT HER LEFT, or displace the uterus left by hand — SECONDS, no equipment · spinal precautions? TILT THE WHOLE DEVICE · DIAPHRAGM PUSHED UP → less lung capacity, breathless sooner · SLOWER STOMACH EMPTYING + RELAXED SPHINCTER → HIGHER ASPIRATION RISK · THE UTERUS RISES OUT OF THE PELVIS and becomes the largest UNPROTECTED abdominal structure · TREATING THE MOTHER IS THE ONLY FETAL TREATMENT YOU HAVE
back.why_it_matters: There was no reason for the falling pressure in her injuries. There was one in how she was lying.

front.title: Complications of pregnancy
front.summary: Painless and visible, or painful and hidden

back.body: PRE-ECLAMPSIA: raised pressure + organ involvement, usually SECOND HALF · WARNING SIGNS: HEADACHE · VISUAL DISTURBANCE · UPPER ABDOMINAL PAIN · swelling of face and hands · RISING BP against a normally low baseline — those symptoms late in pregnancy are not 'a headache' · ECLAMPSIA = progression to SEIZURES, life-threatening for both · MANAGE: airway · oxygen · LEFT SIDE · QUIET AND DIM, minimal handling — LIGHT, NOISE AND HANDLING PROVOKE FURTHER SEIZURES, so turning the lights down IS an intervention · PREVIA: placenta over the cervix — PAINLESS, bright red, VISIBLE · ABRUPTION: placenta separating — PAINFUL, tense abdomen, BLEEDING MAY BE CONCEALED · NEVER PERFORM A VAGINAL EXAMINATION ON A BLEEDING PREGNANT PATIENT
back.why_it_matters: They dimmed everything and handled her minimally. There was not a third seizure.

back.body: See the comparison rows. The pair in one line: PREVIA IS PAINLESS BLEEDING YOU CAN SEE; ABRUPTION IS PAINFUL BLEEDING YOU MAY NOT. Shock out of proportion to visible loss is characteristic of abruption. NEITHER gets a vaginal examination, ever.
back.why_it_matters: In abruption, what you can see tells you nothing about what has been lost.

back.body: THREE STAGES: FIRST = contractions DILATING THE CERVIX (longest, usually the transport stage) · SECOND = DELIVERY OF THE BABY · THIRD = delivery of the PLACENTA · BUT THE DECISION YOU ACTUALLY MAKE IS: TRANSPORT, OR DELIVER HERE? · DELIVER HERE IF: CROWNING — which is delivery HAPPENING, not approaching · contractions CLOSE TOGETHER and STRONG · AN URGE TO PUSH — physiological, not a preference · a feeling of needing to open her bowels (head pressure — reliable and easily dismissed) · ASK TWO THINGS: HOW MANY BABIES BEFORE? (second and later come FASTER — first-baby timelines do not apply) and WHAT ARE THE CONTRACTIONS DOING? (length and interval, not how painful) · PREPARE EARLY — standing down beats catching up
back.why_it_matters: She had done this three times before and said it was coming now. She had better data than they did.

back.body: THE MOTHER DELIVERS THE BABY — you GUIDE, SUPPORT, CONTROL THE SPEED and CATCH · SUPPORT THE HEAD with a flat hand, let it come SLOWLY — you control speed, NOT direction · AS SOON AS THE HEAD IS OUT, FEEL FOR THE CORD AROUND THE NECK — common, usually loose, SLIP IT OVER · TIGHT AND UNFREEABLE: CLAMP TWICE, CUT BETWEEN, deliver immediately (know if your protocol permits it, and where your clamps are) · LET THE HEAD ROTATE on its own · GUIDE GENTLY DOWN for the upper shoulder, GENTLY UP for the lower · THE BODY COMES FAST AND EXTREMELY SLIPPERY — firm grip, TOWEL ALREADY IN HAND · DRY VIGOROUSLY (warms AND stimulates) · KEEP WARM, COVER THE HEAD · NOTE THE TIME · NEVER PULL THE CORD — it can INVERT THE UTERUS · Do not wait for the placenta
back.why_it_matters: The body came out in about a second and a half. Nobody tells you how slippery they are.

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: crowning means DELIVER HERE · PREPARE EARLY · full splash PPE · SUPPORT THE HEAD and control the SPEED · CHECK FOR A NUCHAL CORD as soon as the head is out · slip loose cords over, CLAMP TWICE AND CUT a tight one · let the head rotate · UPPER SHOULDER DOWN, LOWER SHOULDER UP · expect a fast slippery body with the towel already in hand · DRY VIGOROUSLY · KEEP WARM, COVER THE HEAD · NOTE THE TIME · NEVER PULL THE CORD · do not wait for the placenta.
back.why_it_matters: Everything here is either controlling the speed or not dropping the baby.

back.body: ALL OF THEM: RAPID TRANSPORT + PRE-ALERT — they need a theatre · PROLAPSED CORD: the presenting part COMPRESSES the cord, which is the baby's ENTIRE oxygen supply → HEAD DOWN, HIPS UP · GLOVED HAND IN · LIFT THE PRESENTING PART OFF THE CORD · AND DO NOT LET GO — through the carry, the loading, the drive and the handover · DO NOT PUSH THE CORD BACK · keep it warm and moist · high-flow O2 to the mother · BREECH: support what delivers, NEVER PULL — traction traps the head · HEAD NOT DELIVERING? TWO FINGERS IN A V BESIDE THE FACE to make an airway, hold it, GO · NUCHAL CORD: slip it over if loose, CLAMP TWICE AND CUT if tight · SHOULDER DYSTOCIA: time-critical, positional manoeuvres per protocol, NO TRACTION ON THE HEAD
back.why_it_matters: That hand had been the baby's entire oxygen supply for half an hour.

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: recognise it, START MOVING AND PRE-ALERT, HEAD DOWN WITH HIPS UP, GLOVED HAND IN LIFTING THE PRESENTING PART OFF THE CORD, DO NOT LET GO for anything, do NOT push the cord back, keep it warm and moist, high-flow oxygen to the mother, transport rapidly, and HAND OVER WITH YOUR HAND STILL IN PLACE.
back.why_it_matters: In this one emergency, your hand is not assisting the treatment. It is the treatment.

back.body: EXCESSIVE BLEEDING AFTER DELIVERY — a leading cause of maternal death, and it can be sudden and large · COMMONEST CAUSE BY FAR: A UTERUS THAT HAS NOT CONTRACTED — after the placenta separates the site is a large raw area of OPEN VESSELS, and the ONLY thing that closes them is the uterus SQUEEZING · FEEL THE FUNDUS: FIRM = contracted · SOFT AND BOGGY = your finding · TREATMENT: FIRM CIRCULAR UTERINE MASSAGE — effective, needs NO equipment, and gets skipped because it feels invasive · Explain it and do it · BREASTFEEDING stimulates contraction, if she is willing · LOSS IS ROUTINELY UNDERESTIMATED — spread across bedding, and pregnancy hypervolaemia means SHE LOOKS WELL UNTIL SHE DOES NOT · NEVER PACK THE VAGINA — external pads, counted · Treat as SHOCK · do not wait for the placenta
back.why_it_matters: It firmed up under her hand and the bleeding slowed within a minute.

back.body: ALMOST EVERY NEWBORN NEEDS THREE THINGS: WARM · DRY · STIMULATE — and VIGOROUS DRYING DOES ALL THREE AT ONCE · They lose heat FRIGHTENINGLY FAST: dry, REMOVE THE WET TOWEL, wrap, COVER THE HEAD · THREE QUESTIONS DECIDE EVERYTHING: is it TERM? is it BREATHING OR CRYING? does it have GOOD TONE? · ALL THREE YES → dry, warm, GIVE IT TO ITS MOTHER, skin to skin — that is the whole intervention and it beats anything else · ANY NO → resuscitation · APGAR at ONE and FIVE minutes: Appearance · Pulse · Grimace · Activity · Respiration, 0–2 each, out of 10 · IT DOCUMENTS PROGRESS AND NEVER DIRECTS OR DELAYS RESUSCITATION · THE HEART RATE IS THE MOST USEFUL NUMBER — cord base or stethoscope
back.why_it_matters: Both of them had their hands on the baby. The score was written down afterwards and changed nothing.

front.title: APGAR
front.summary: Scored at one minute and five

back.body: A — APPEARANCE: 0 blue/pale all over · 1 body pink, extremities blue · 2 pink all over · P — PULSE: 0 absent · 1 below 100 · 2 above 100 · G — GRIMACE: 0 no response · 1 grimace · 2 cry, cough or sneeze · A — ACTIVITY: 0 limp · 1 some flexion · 2 active movement · R — RESPIRATION: 0 absent · 1 slow, irregular or weak cry · 2 strong cry · TOTAL out of 10, at ONE minute and FIVE — the COMPARISON is the useful part · IT NEVER DIRECTS RESUSCITATION AND NEVER DELAYS IT
back.why_it_matters: Ventilate the baby. Write the score afterwards.

front.title: Neonatal resuscitation
front.summary: A breathing problem, not a heart problem

back.body: NEWBORN RESUSCITATION IS A BREATHING PROBLEM — the heart is usually fine and is failing for want of oxygen, which REVERSES the adult priority · VENTILATION IS THE INTERVENTION, and the one most often started TOO LATE · WARM, DRY, STIMULATE → POSITION NEUTRAL (pad the shoulders) → CLEAR ONLY IF OBSTRUCTED → ASSESS BREATHING AND HEART RATE · NOT BREATHING, GASPING, OR HR BELOW 100 → VENTILATE · IS IT WORKING? CHEST RISE and A RISING HEART RATE — the heart rate is the better indicator · LOOK AT THE CHEST, NOT AT THE BAG · No rise? REPOSITION, SEAL, OBSTRUCTION — before anything else · HR STILL BELOW 60 AFTER 30 SECONDS OF EFFECTIVE VENTILATION → COMPRESSIONS AT 3:1, two thumbs encircling · KEEP IT WARM THROUGHOUT
back.why_it_matters: They looked at the chest rather than the bag. The heart rate climbed within fifteen seconds.

back.body: See the skill card steps. Critical: WARM DRY STIMULATE (enough for most), remove the wet towel and COVER THE HEAD, NEUTRAL airway with shoulder padding, suction ONLY if obstructed, assess BREATHING AND HEART RATE, VENTILATE if apnoeic/gasping/HR<100, confirm CHEST RISE and a RISING HEART RATE, fix position and seal before escalating, COMPRESSIONS AT 3:1 if HR<60 after 30 SECONDS OF EFFECTIVE VENTILATION, reassess the heart rate, keep warm.
back.why_it_matters: Everything here is ventilation until the heart rate says otherwise.

back.body: EVERYTHING THAT MAKES A NEWBORN VULNERABLE IS EXAGGERATED · HEAT LOSS IS THE BIGGEST IMMEDIATE PROBLEM — less fat, thinner skin, bigger relative surface area; cold worsens breathing, circulation, clotting AND resuscitation · warm the ambulance past your own comfort · IMMATURE LUNGS → far more likely to need ventilation, so be ready BEFORE you need to be · FRAGILE — handle gently; ordinary handling IS significant stimulation · More prone to INFECTION — clean technique · CORRECT EQUIPMENT SIZE: A MASK THAT DOES NOT SEAL DOES NOT VENTILATE — know what you carry and where, before 3am in a bathroom · SAME RESUSCITATION SEQUENCE · DO NOT JUDGE VIABILITY ON SCENE — start, continue, transport, and let people with the gestation and the weight decide · Neonatal capability + PRE-ALERT
back.why_it_matters: Nobody on that floor knew the gestation within four weeks. That decision belonged elsewhere.

back.body: HOW YOU APPROACH DECIDES HOW MUCH ASSESSMENT YOU GET · GET DOWN TO THEIR EYE LEVEL — an adult in uniform standing over a small child is an intimidating shape · KEEP THE CHILD WITH THE CAREGIVER — a child in a parent's arms tolerates what the same child alone will fight · CALMING THE PARENT IS A CLINICAL INTERVENTION: their state goes straight into the child · ASSESS TOE TO HEAD in small children, saving the face and airway for LAST · INFANTS: warmth, gentleness, a familiar voice — not explanation · TODDLERS: fear SEPARATION and STRANGERS, take language LITERALLY — concrete words, let them touch kit, offer choices that do not matter · SCHOOL AGE: explain first, be honest · ADOLESCENTS: privacy, dignity, spoken TO not about · NEVER TELL A CHILD SOMETHING WILL NOT HURT WHEN IT WILL
back.why_it_matters: Two crews tried from standing. The third sat on the floor and started with a shoe.

back.body: BIG HEAD, PROMINENT OCCIPUT → the neck FLEXES when supine → PAD UNDER THE SHOULDERS (opposite of the adult) · BIGGER TONGUE, NARROWER, SOFTER, COLLAPSIBLE AIRWAY — OVER-EXTENSION KINKS IT SHUT · A SMALL AMOUNT OF SWELLING TAKES A LARGE SHARE OF A SMALL AIRWAY · HORIZONTAL, CARTILAGINOUS RIBS → DIAPHRAGM DEPENDENT (a distended stomach impairs breathing) and FORCE PASSES THROUGH TO THE ORGANS WITH NO FRACTURE · A RIB FRACTURE IN A CHILD MEANS ENORMOUS FORCE · BIG SURFACE AREA → COOLS FAST, including mid-resuscitation · MORE BLOOD PER KILO BUT MUCH LESS IN TOTAL — judge the loss against the size of the patient · LIVER AND SPLEEN large and poorly protected · THEY COMPENSATE BEAUTIFULLY THEN FALL OFF A CLIFF
back.why_it_matters: The ribs bent and sprang back. The lungs underneath took all of it.

back.body: A STRUCTURED GENERAL IMPRESSION formed ACROSS THE ROOM, NO EQUIPMENT, BEFORE YOU TOUCH THE CHILD · It answers HOW SICK and WHICH SYSTEM · APPEARANCE — is the BRAIN PERFUSED AND OXYGENATED? TICLS: Tone · Interactiveness · Consolability · Look or gaze · Speech or cry · WORK OF BREATHING — stridor, grunting, wheeze; tripoding, sniffing, refusing to lie down; retractions; nasal flaring; head bobbing · CIRCULATION TO THE SKIN — pallor, mottling, cyanosis · THE QUIET CHILD IS THE TRAP: a screaming child is spending energy and interacting; a FLOPPY SILENT child who does not mind a stranger is usually SICKER · A CHILD NOT BEHAVING LIKE A CHILD IS A SICK CHILD, whatever the numbers say
back.why_it_matters: When did you last meet a well two year old who let a stranger do everything?

back.body: APPEARANCE = TICLS: Tone, Interactiveness, Consolability, Look or gaze, Speech or cry · WORK OF BREATHING = sounds, position, retractions, flaring, head bobbing · CIRCULATION TO SKIN = pallor, mottling, cyanosis · PATTERNS: breathing only → RESPIRATORY DISTRESS · breathing + appearance → RESPIRATORY FAILURE · appearance + skin, breathing normal → SHOCK · all three → CARDIOPULMONARY FAILURE · Costs a few seconds and no equipment, and supplements rather than replaces the primary assessment
back.why_it_matters: Silence is not settled.

back.body: RESPIRATORY FAILURE IS THE COMMONEST ROUTE TO PAEDIATRIC ARREST — catch it and you prevent the arrest · DISTRESS = working hard and SUCCEEDING: retractions, nasal flaring, grunting, noisy breathing, tripoding or sniffing, refusing to lie down, FAST rate, ALERT AND FRIGHTENED · FAILURE = working hard and LOSING, and IT LOOKS QUIETER: effort DECREASING (exhausted), chest going QUIET (less air moving, NOT improvement), tone DECREASING, MENTAL STATUS ALTERED, HEART RATE FALLING — bradycardia is VERY LATE AND VERY OMINOUS · EVERY SIGN THAT LOOKS LIKE IMPROVEMENT IS ON THE FAILURE LIST · Let them keep their chosen position · KEEP THEM CALM — crying can tip a marginal child over · FAILURE → ASSIST VENTILATION, do not wait for arrest
back.why_it_matters: The wheeze had settled because almost nothing was moving.

front.summary: Working and winning, working and losing

back.body: CHILDREN COMPENSATE EXCEPTIONALLY WELL — which is exactly what makes this dangerous · THEY HOLD A NORMAL-LOOKING BLOOD PRESSURE UNTIL COMPENSATION FAILS, SO HYPOTENSION IS LATE AND OMINOUS · NEVER LET A NORMAL BP REASSURE YOU · EARLY SIGNS ARE PERIPHERAL AND BEHAVIOURAL: TACHYCARDIA (non-specific), PROLONGED CAPILLARY REFILL, COOL PALE THEN MOTTLED SKIN, WEAK PERIPHERAL PULSES WITH STRONG CENTRAL ONES — feel both deliberately · ALTERED APPEARANCE = the brain noticing poor perfusion first · ASK ABOUT WET NAPPIES vs a normal day · DEHYDRATION from vomiting and diarrhoea is common and undramatic · JUDGE BLOOD LOSS AGAINST THE SIZE OF THE PATIENT, NOT THE PUDDLE · Oxygen per protocol, control bleeding, KEEP WARM, TRANSPORT
back.why_it_matters: The skin was mottled to the knees. They treated that and ignored the number.

back.body: PROTECT FROM INJURY · DO NOT RESTRAIN · NOTHING IN THE MOUTH · protect the head, clear the space, NOTE THE TIME AND WHAT YOU SAW; afterwards POSITION FOR AIRWAY, suction, oxygen per protocol · FEBRILE SEIZURES: young children, a RISING temperature (the rise matters more than the peak), usually BRIEF, GENERALISED AND SELF-LIMITING · USUALLY BENIGN FOR THE CHILD AND TERRIFYING FOR THE CAREGIVER — treat both · EVERY CHILD WHO HAS SEIZED IS TRANSPORTED, because the CAUSE is what matters · KEEP A DIFFERENTIAL: HEAD INJURY · LOW BLOOD SUGAR · POISONING · INFECTION · HYPOXIA · COOL SENSIBLY: remove clothing, NO ICE, COLD WATER OR ALCOHOL (shivering raises temperature) · POSTICTAL DROWSINESS IS EXPECTED — not improving, repeating without recovery, or not stopping is an EMERGENCY
back.why_it_matters: One of them sat with the mother and explained it twice. That was the treatment that call needed.

back.body: SUDDEN INFANT DEATH: sudden, UNEXPLAINED death of an infant, typically found during sleep — NOT something you diagnose on scene · BEGIN RESUSCITATION unless there are obvious signs of irreversible death, per protocol · DO NOT SPECULATE ABOUT CAUSE and NEVER SUGGEST OR IMPLY BLAME, including by how you ask questions · OBSERVE AND DOCUMENT FACTUALLY: POSITION FOUND · bedding and sleep surface · objects · who else was in the bed · room temperature · TIME LAST SEEN WELL and by whom · DOCUMENT WHAT YOU OBSERVE, NOT WHAT YOU CONCLUDE · THE CREW NEEDS SUPPORT AFTERWARDS · BRUE: a resolved episode of COLOUR, TONE, BREATHING or RESPONSIVENESS change — A NORMAL-LOOKING INFANT STILL NEEDS TRANSPORT, and the caregiver's account is taken seriously
back.why_it_matters: You are the only clinician who will ever see that room as it was.

back.body: EMS ARE MANDATED REPORTERS IN MOST SYSTEMS — know your obligation and your procedure BEFORE you need it · YOU REPORT SUSPICION, NOT PROOF — you are not the investigator · STRONGEST INDICATOR: A HISTORY THAT DOES NOT MATCH THE INJURY · also a CHANGING history, a DELAY in seeking care, an injury IMPOSSIBLE FOR THE CHILD'S DEVELOPMENTAL STAGE · FINDINGS: unusual locations (not shins, knees, elbows, foreheads), PATTERNED injuries, injuries of CLEARLY DIFFERENT AGES, unusual burns · NEGLECT: hygiene, malnutrition, untreated conditions, unsafe environment · DO NOT CONFRONT OR ACCUSE — it endangers the child, the crew, and the transport · YOUR JOB: CARE · TRANSPORT · FACTUAL DOCUMENTATION with QUOTES attributed and injuries described, NOT interpreted · Reporting in good faith is legally protected
back.why_it_matters: The story was that the infant rolled off the sofa. The infant was not yet rolling over.

cards.verify_notes: Drafted from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level) and not yet reviewed against a source text, same as its parent concept EMT-07-03-08. Check every figure on this card against the source before it is printed or drilled.

back.body: Trauma is a LEADING CAUSE OF DEATH in children and the mechanisms are overwhelmingly BLUNT · A SMALLER BODY SPREADS THE SAME FORCE ACROSS MORE OF IT → MULTI-SYSTEM INJURY IS THE NORM — look everywhere, always · THE HEAD IS LARGE, HEAVY AND LEADS IN A FALL — head injury is common and often the most significant thing present; WATCH MENTAL STATUS · FLEXIBLE BONES AND RIBS TRANSMIT FORCE TO ORGANS WITHOUT BREAKING — NO FRACTURE IS NOT REASSURANCE · ASSUME THE MECHANISM: treat what the force COULD have done, not what you can see · AIRWAY: NEUTRAL, PAD THE SHOULDERS, DO NOT OVER-EXTEND · KEEP THEM WARM — hypothermia worsens bleeding · JUDGE BLOOD LOSS AGAINST PATIENT SIZE · DECIDE TRANSPORT EARLY, ON MECHANISM — they compensate then crash · Paediatric-capable destination + pre-alert
back.why_it_matters: They made the decision on the mechanism. That is the only time you get to make it early.
